speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: asked the Minister for Law what is the rationale for the new pre-Court action protocol for business-to-business debt claims and whether the Government has consulted businesses prior to introducing the new Court protocol.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It was implemented in August 2019 by an amendment to the State Courts Practice Directions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These Practice Directions (PDs) are issued by the Court to regulate its practice and procedure and are updated from time to time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new Protocol seeks to encourage businesses to resolve their debt claims early, before the commencement of proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Approximately 75% of those claims, however, are eventually withdrawn, discontinued or have judgments entered in default.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Based on the State Courts' experience, this is because such claims are frequently brought even though the debt is not disputed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Rather, the claims may be brought because there is poor documentation, wrong calculation of interest, or the debtor was simply seeking a breakdown of the debt or a repayment plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As a result, costs incurred for the legal proceedings are very often disproportionate to the claimed sums and Court resources are also being utilised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new Protocol was, therefore, introduced with the objectives of: (a) helping parties to identify the quantum of the claim, including interest, the relevant documents which may support the substantiation of the claim, and identifying the issues in dispute; (b) encouraging early communications between parties, active exploration of Alternative Dispute Resolution options, and the upfront exchange of documents and information; and (c) where legal proceedings cannot be avoided, the new Protocol will facilitate the drafting of proper pleadings and ensure that documentation is in order, as well as help to narrow the issues in dispute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will focus the parties and also reduce the length of Court proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under the new Protocol, a Letter of Claim is sent prior to commencing legal proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Letter must contain details of the claim, such as the amount of debt and applicable interest, as well as the underlying agreement giving rise to the claim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The debtor is then required to send a Response to the Letter of Claim within 28 days, or such shorter timeframe as may be appropriate depending on the circumstances of each case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new Protocol does not bar any creditor from bringing legal proceedings on an outstanding debt claim at any point in time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The State Courts hold regular engagements with the Law Society and the members of the Bar on a variety of civil matters, including proposed changes to civil procedure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The State Courts previously discussed the new Protocol with the Law Society’s Civil Practice Committee, whose members represent both creditors and debtors, the business-to-business aspect to which the Protocol applies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Since implementation, the State Courts further engaged the Law Society earlier this year on 14 January 2020 and solicited their written feedback on the Protocol as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Law Society provided its feedback in writing to the State Courts on 28 January 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The State Courts will be studying this feedback with a view to finetuning the Protocol, as may be appropriate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am sure the Senior Minister of State is fully aware that most lawyers already issue demand letters with at least seven days' notice.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In this case, the Protocol specifies a notice period of 28 days.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And how does the Court then balance the fact that some debtors do drag their feet and refuse to pay until they are sued in Court?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, how does the Court then consider the interest of creditors who are in that situation?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The only question is, at the time of reckoning, which I think Mr Lim Biow Chuan would be aware, is actually different from the position today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Even as we assess the conduct of parties, it is to assess whether or not the action has been reasonable or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in doing so, the Court will consider a series of circumstances, including those that I have outlined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is how the Courts will then strike a balance between ensuring that the creditor has sufficient time to make known the nature of the claim, make known the details to support the claim so that the debtor can decide if he wants to enter into Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR), for instance, or maybe he decides to then seek upfront, the repayment plan from the creditor.
